rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - authors built a mobile drip line with Arduino control and ran laboratory calibration and uniformity tests (Figures 7-11), reporting their own CUC, application efficiency and speed data.
rows.notes: The study contains no AI, predictive analytics, real-time weather or soil-moisture sensing, or scheduling app. Required depths were pre-computed from ETo and Kc and loaded onto an SD card. The 'up to 30% water reduction' is not reported; the study gives a calculated potential saving of 23.2% (or at least 19.1%) for variable-rate versus constant-rate application, derived from the difference between average and maximum required depths in a lab test, not from an AI-driven scheduling system.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory tests of a mobile drip line (pulse-valve calibration, constant- and variable-rate uniformity tests, speed and pressure-loss measurements).
rows.notes: The study is a drip-based system, but its only water-use result is a computed potential saving (23.2%, or at least 19.1%) of variable-rate application relative to a hypothetical constant-rate application at maximum demand (Section 3.3, Figure 10). This contrast isolates variable-rate control, not drip irrigation itself, and is an arithmetic estimate from required depths in a laboratory simulation of crop demands rather than a measured water-use outcome of drip versus another method. No IoT, AI or remote-sensing integration beyond a radio link between two Arduino panels. Doubt noted: a lenient reader might treat the automated drip line as a 'smart drip system', but the saving is attributed to variable rate, so answered no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory development and performance tests of the drip line.
rows.notes: No remote sensing of any kind is used or tested; crop water needs were entered manually from ETo and Kc tables (Table 1). Remote sensing is only mentioned when citing another study [26] in the Discussion. The study provides no own evidence on remote sensing and water conservation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory development and performance tests of the drip line.
rows.notes: The study has no scheduling app or decision-support software; depths and positions are pre-loaded on an SD card and the controller only computes line speed and valve activation times. Water savings reported (23.2% potential) are a calculated comparison of variable- versus constant-rate depths, not an outcome of app-based scheduling.

notes: Full text available and readable despite some duplicated/garbled layout lines from PDF extraction. The study is a laboratory engineering evaluation of a mobile variable-rate drip line (CUC, application efficiency, speed stability, pressure loss); it is not a field trial and contains no AI, remote sensing, soil-moisture sensing or scheduling application. The 23.2%/19.1% 'potential water savings' is computed from the spread of required depths, with the authors themselves stating further study is needed to quantify resource savings.
